documents.unit: Office of the Provost / Faculty Senate
documents.title: Code of Academic Integrity
documents.summary: UVM's Code of Academic Integrity is a general conduct code, and its one AI-specific line sits inside the cheating standard. Work generated by AI is not counted as the student's own and is not permitted unless the instructor expressly says so. The rest of the code is process: who reports, how hearings work, sanctions.
documents.stance_why: The cheating standard says 'Work generated by artificial intelligence is not considered to be created by the student and is not permitted unless expressly stated by the instructor.' AI is banned by default and allowed only where an instructor says so, which is restrict. It does not delegate the default to instructors, because the ban applies unless an exception is stated.

units.why: The cheating standard says AI-generated work 'is not permitted unless expressly stated by the instructor', which sets a default ban with an instructor exception. I chose P01 (default ban) rather than P06 because it is the standing rule of the Code, not a statement about what happens when a syllabus is silent.
units.anchor: is not permitted unless expressly stated by the instructor
units.policy: Work generated by artificial intelligence is not permitted unless expressly stated by the instructor.

units.why: 'Work generated by artificial intelligence is not considered to be created by the student' defines AI output as not the student's own work, which is why it is barred. It is coded P19 because the point is that AI may not produce what a student submits as their own.
units.anchor: Work generated by artificial intelligence is not considered to be created by the student

units.why: 'Students may not claim as their own work any portion of academic work that was not created by the student' is a general ownership rule that the Code applies to AI. P29 fits because it requires submitted work to be the student's own.
units.anchor: Students may not claim as their own work any portion of academic work that was

units.why: 'Students must adhere to the guidelines for completing academic work provided by their instructors' makes instructor rules binding, which includes any AI rule. P78 fits because students must follow the rules that apply in each course.
units.anchor: Students must adhere to the guidelines for completing academic work provided by their instructors

units.why: 'Students may only use materials approved by their instructor when completing an assignment or exam' means unapproved resources, which would include AI, are not allowed. It is not AI-specific, so P06 (unless allowed, not permitted) is only a partial fit.
units.anchor: Students may only use materials approved by their instructor when completing an assignment or exam
units.fit_note: The sentence does not mention AI or a silent syllabus; it limits all materials to those the instructor approves.

units.why: 'Course expectations may vary from instructor to instructor' says that rules, including for AI, are set course by course. P04 fits because the decision is left to each instructor.
units.anchor: Course expectations may vary from instructor to instructor

units.why: 'All students have an obligation to ensure a clear understanding of the expectations associated with each particular assignment and each particular course' puts the duty to learn the rules on students. P78 is chosen over P10 because it is a general duty and does not say to ask when unsure.
units.anchor: All students have an obligation to ensure a clear understanding of the expectations

units.why: 'Violations of this standard constitute cheating' places violations of the cheating standard, which contains the AI sentence, under academic dishonesty. P36 fits as AI use the instructor has not allowed is handled as misconduct.
units.anchor: Violations of this standard constitute cheating
units.fit_note: The sentence does not name AI itself; AI follows through the cheating standard in the same paragraph.

units.why: 'Faculty are encouraged to refer to the Code of Academic Integrity on course syllabi and to discuss the standards of academic integrity and their expectations at the start of the semester' asks instructors to communicate integrity rules at the start. P09 is the nearest type, but it covers integrity in general rather than AI.
units.anchor: Faculty are encouraged to refer to the Code of Academic Integrity on course syllabi
units.fit_note: Asks for a reference to the Code and a start-of-term discussion, not an AI statement in particular.

units.why: 'All suspected deliberate violations of academic integrity (plagiarism, fabrication, collusion, or cheating) must be reported to the Center for Student Conduct within two weeks of discovery' sets the reporting duty that applies to AI cheating. P81 fits because it is a required reporting step with a deadline.
units.anchor: must be reported to the Center for Student Conduct within two weeks of discovery

units.why: 'Faculty may recommend a sanction, however, the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee or the Academic Integrity Council will make the final sanction determination' leaves sanctions to the deciding body. P81 fits as a procedural step.
units.anchor: Faculty may recommend a sanction, however, the Coordinator of Academic Integrity

units.why: 'For a first offense, an undergraduate student will likely receive a grade of XF in the indicated course' states a concrete penalty in advance that applies to AI cheating. P37 fits because the penalty and its escalation by offense are named.
units.anchor: For a first offense, an undergraduate student will likely receive a grade of XF

units.why: 'The Respondent will be presumed "not responsible" until proven otherwise by a preponderance standard' sets the standard of proof for integrity findings. P69 fits because it states what evidence level is required.
units.anchor: will be presumed "not responsible" until proven otherwise by a preponderance standard
units.fit_note: Sets a general standard of proof; it does not mention AI evidence or detectors.

units.why: 'Students have a right to an Academic Integrity Council meeting when accused of and subject to penalty for violating the Code' gives accused students a hearing. P64 fits because it is a right to respond to an allegation.
units.anchor: Students have a right to an Academic Integrity Council meeting when accused

units.why: 'Is the incident a technical violation in which there is no perceived intent to achieve an unfair academic advantage?' lists a mitigating factor, so sanctions can be lighter without intent. P68 is closest as it favors a proportionate response, though it is not specifically educative.
units.anchor: Is the incident a technical violation in which there is no perceived intent to achieve
units.fit_note: A mitigating factor in sanctioning; it does not say the response should be educative.

units.why: 'educational sanctions, which may include: A reflective essay or a research paper on principles of academic integrity' offers remedial sanctions instead of only grade penalties. P68 fits because misuse can be answered with learning-oriented sanctions.
units.anchor: A reflective essay or a research paper on principles of academic integrity

units.why: 'If the Coordinator of Academic Integrity or designee believes alleged violations can be resolved via an alternative resolution process (e.g., conflict coaching, mediation, facilitated dialogue or a restorative practice), that option will be explored' makes restorative resolution possible. P68 fits as a non-punitive response.
units.anchor: alleged violations can be resolved via an alternative resolution process

documents.title: About AI at UVM
documents.summary: A short advisory page that defines AI terms and lists five considerations: integrity and transparency, privacy, ethics, and ongoing learning. It sets no binding rules and says nothing about courses or instructors.
documents.stance_why: The page says AI 'is a powerful tool that can be used for learning, productivity, and creativity' and only advises being transparent and avoiding sensitive data. It neither bans AI nor hands decisions to instructors, so permit with conditions is the closest stance; the conditions are advisory ('it is helpful to let others know').

units.why: The page defines AI ('a broad, interdisciplinary field that focuses on designing systems that are capable of performing tasks that typically require human intelligence') to set what the guidance covers. P61 fits as it is a definition of a term.
units.anchor: a broad, interdisciplinary field that focuses on designing systems

units.why: 'ML is a subfield of AI that develops algorithms and statistical models' is a definition of machine learning. P61 fits as a definition that frames the site's scope.
units.anchor: ML is a subfield of AI that develops algorithms and statistical models

units.why: 'Deep learning is a subfield of machine learning that uses multi-layered artificial neural networks' is a definition. P61 fits.
units.anchor: Deep learning is a subfield of machine learning that uses multi-layered artificial neural networks

units.why: 'Generative AI encompasses models and systems designed to produce novel content, such as text, images, audio, or code' defines the tool class that most course policies target. P61 fits.
units.anchor: Generative AI encompasses models and systems designed to produce novel content

units.why: 'AI agents are systems that perceive their environment, make decisions, and take actions to achieve specific goals' defines agents, so the site's scope includes autonomous systems. P61 fits.
units.anchor: AI agents are systems that perceive their environment, make decisions, and take actions

units.why: 'AI is evolving quickly, and so are our conversations about how to use it well. This site will continue to grow' says the guidance will change. P54 fits because it is a statement that the guidance is provisional.
units.anchor: This site will continue to grow along with our community's understanding and needs

units.why: 'Below are some guiding ideas and considerations drawn from ongoing discussions within higher education' presents the list as advisory principles, not rules. P56 fits as a framing preamble for responsible use.
units.anchor: Below are some guiding ideas and considerations drawn from ongoing discussions within higher education

units.why: 'AI is a powerful tool that can be used for learning, productivity, and creativity' states benefits of AI for learning without making a rule. P87 fits.
units.anchor: AI is a powerful tool that can be used for learning, productivity, and creativity

units.why: 'Being transparent about when and how you use AI tools, such as ChatGPT, can help maintain trust and clarity in academic work' recommends disclosure. P24 fits, and the wording is advisory ('can help'), so the modality is should.
units.anchor: Being transparent about when and how you use AI tools, such as ChatGPT, can help

units.why: 'it is helpful to let others know' when AI is involved in writing, coding, analysis or planning extends disclosure to all kinds of work, including code. P24 fits and the advice is non-binding, so should.
units.anchor: it is helpful to let others know

units.why: 'it is wise to avoid sharing any personal, confidential, or sensitive information' with AI systems that 'store and process user inputs'. P50 fits because it protects personal data.
units.anchor: it is wise to avoid sharing any personal, confidential, or sensitive information

units.why: 'AI can support your work, but it shouldn't replace thoughtful judgment' keeps the human as decision-maker. P32 fits.
units.anchor: it shouldn't replace thoughtful judgment

units.why: AI should not 'be used to mislead' is a conduct rule against deceptive use. P74 fits because it bans deceptive use in general.
units.anchor: or be used to mislead

units.why: 'AI-generated content can also contain bias and error, so it is important to consider how this may affect your conclusions' asks users to weigh errors and bias. P31 fits.
units.anchor: AI-generated content can also contain bias and error

units.why: 'Staying curious and informed helps us all engage with these tools in more meaningful and responsible ways' encourages users to keep up. P102 fits.
units.anchor: Staying curious and informed helps us all engage with these tools

documents.title: Teaching and Writing in the Age of AI
tiers: AI assistance allowed, text generation not
documents.summary: Faculty guidance from Writing in the Disciplines on addressing AI in courses. It says every instructor must state AI expectations, and gives sample syllabus statements at five levels from allowed-with-attribution to prohibited. It also covers assignment redesign, the limits of detectors, and a catalogue of AI writing tools. It is not computing-specific.
documents.stance_why: The page says 'each of us must specifically address AI on multiple levels' and offers sample statements for 'generally allowed with attribution', 'prior permission', 'specific assignments' and 'generally prohibited'. It sets no AI rule of its own beyond pointing to the Code, so the decision goes to instructors; the tiers are listed in the tiers field.

units.anchor: each of us must specifically address AI on multiple levels

units.why: 'Students report that the widespread lack of information about AI on syllabi creates confusion and uncertainty' gives the reason for stating AI policy. P09 fits as the rationale for the syllabus-statement expectation.
units.anchor: the widespread lack of information about AI on syllabi creates confusion and uncertainty

units.why: 'even that statement may not address all questions related to your class' says the Code's AI line is not enough and instructors need their own policy. P09 fits.
units.anchor: even that statement may not address all questions related to your class

units.why: 'We have options for weaving AI use and AI critical literacy into our assignments' says instructors may design assignments that include AI. P35 fits.
units.anchor: We have options for weaving AI use and AI critical literacy into our assignments

units.anchor: Easy access to AI upends traditional approaches to assessment security

units.anchor: the implementation of its principles may vary from course to course

units.anchor: instructors must be clear about what they expect about the use of AI

documents.title: Understanding Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI)
documents.summary: A student-facing Writing Center guide to generative AI. It tells students to follow each instructor's policy and ask when unsure, explains limits, risks and citation, and lists writing uses with advice to stay in charge. It covers writing, not code.
documents.stance_why: The guide says 'pay attention to the policies your instructors have established in their courses' and quotes the Code that AI is 'not permitted unless expressly stated by the instructor'. It sets no rule of its own and sends students to instructor policies, so delegates; it also lists permissible writing uses, but only as options.

units.why: 'help you as a student writer to understand how GenAI works and to shape your decisions about whether, when, or how to use it' states the guide's purpose. P56 fits as a purpose statement.

units.fit_note: Covers risks, ethics and critical thinking generally, not only checking output accuracy.

notes: Only four UVM documents were included. The AI-site sub-pages and the CS1210 syllabus were not coded (empty or deferred). The Code of Academic Integrity has one AI sentence; I coded the AI-related rule, the communication and course-variation sentences, and the reporting, sanction and hearing provisions that apply to AI cheating, and skipped the rest of the hearing procedure as unrelated to AI. WID is a faculty-development unit, so its sample syllabus statements from other universities are coded as the examples they are (the tiers field lists the five levels). In the WID document, the sample statement 'Violations could result in failure of the assignment...' appears in three samples and is coded once. Candidate new type: requirement of prior instructor permission before any AI use (coded UNCOVERED).
